GROUNDS TO CONTEST A WILL OR TRUST — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · March 15, 2026

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the substantive grounds California law recognizes for challenging the validity of a will or trust made by Pat Morgan, who died on March 15, 2026, and the basic procedural rules -- standing and time limits -- for raising such a challenge in Sacramento County County, California. It states facts about California law generally. It does not determine whether any ground for a challenge exists on these particular facts, and it does not advise on whether to bring, join, or forgo a challenge.

GROUND: LACK OF TESTAMENTARY CAPACITY
One recognized ground for contesting the validity of Pat Morgan's will is that Pat Morgan lacked testamentary capacity when it was signed. Under California law, an individual lacks the mental competency required to make a will if, at the time of making it, the individual either did not have sufficient mental capacity to understand the nature of the act of making a will, to understand and recall the nature and extent of the individual's own property, and to remember and understand the individual's relationships with living descendants, spouse, and parents and others affected by the will -- or if the individual suffered from a mental health disorder involving delusions or hallucinations that actually caused a specific distribution the individual would not otherwise have made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "An individual is not mentally competent to make a will if, at the time of making the will, either of the following is true: (1) The individual does not have sufficient mental capacity to be able to do any of the following: (A) Understand the nature of the testamentary act. (B) Understand and recollect the nature and situation of the individual’s property. (C) Remember and understand the individual’s relations to living descendants, spouse, and parents, and those whose interests are affected by the will. (2) The individual suffers from a mental health disorder with symptoms including delusions or hallucinations, which delusions or hallucinations result in the individual’s devising property in a way that, except for the existence of the delusions or hallucinations, the individual would not have done."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6100.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two-part testamentary capacity test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6100.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 6100.5(a)), used as real evidence of the actual legal test a capacity-based contest must satisfy -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This same statutory subsection is already stated elsewhere in this corpus, in a different clause (the Last Will and Testament document's testamentary-capacity clause), framed there as a drafting-time requirement for the will to be valid rather than as a ground a contestant can raise; this clause independently re-verified the identical primary source (fetched and cross-checked again for this document) and restates it framed around a contest instead. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was located for the capacity test itself. This clause does not address the separate, narrower rule that a conservator may make a will for a conservatee only with prior court authorization, and does not state how a capacity-based contest must be pleaded or proven at trial.

GROUNDS: DURESS, MENACE, FRAUD, AND UNDUE INFLUENCE
California law separately recognizes four other grounds for treating a will (or part of one) -- and, under the same statutory language, a revocation of a will -- as invalid: the execution or revocation is ineffective to the extent it was procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence. Unlike the capacity ground, these four grounds go to how Pat Morgan's will, or its revocation, actually came about, rather than to whether Pat Morgan had the mental capacity to make it at all, and by the statute's own wording each ground is effective only to the extent it actually procured the execution or revocation at issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The execution or revocation of a will or a part of a will is ineffective to the extent the execution or revocation was procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6104 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, procurement-based grounds for invalidity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6104.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 6104), used as real evidence of the four procurement-based invalidity grounds -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This is the entire operative text of a single statutory section; there is no subsection breakdown to disclose, and no additional independent source was located for this specific list of four grounds. The statute does not itself define 'duress,' 'menace,' or 'fraud'; this sheet's separate clause on Probate Code section 86 addresses how 'undue influence' is defined for these purposes, but this clause does not independently verify statutory definitions for the other three terms, which are left to case law.

HOW "UNDUE INFLUENCE" IS DEFINED FOR A WILL OR TRUST CONTEST
California Probate Code section 86 answers the definitional question left open by the previous clause: for purposes of the Probate Code, "undue influence" has the same meaning given to that term in Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70. The Legislature's own statement of intent is that this cross-reference supplements the pre-existing common-law meaning of undue influence, rather than replacing or overriding it. So a contest raising undue influence as a ground can draw on both that statutory definition and the body of case law that predates and coexists with it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Undue influence” has the same meaning as defined in Section 15610.70 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. It is the intent of the Legislature that this section supplement the common law meaning of undue influence without superseding or interfering with the operation of that law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 86 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, definition of "undue influence" by cross-reference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=86.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 86), used as real evidence that the Probate Code defines 'undue influence' by cross-reference to Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70, rather than leaving the term wholly undefined in this context -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not a restatement of section 15610.70's own definition. That definition, and its four evidentiary factors, is already stated in this corpus's separate elder-financial-abuse clause citing Welf. & Inst. Code section 15610.70 directly; this clause does not requote that text, to avoid duplicating it, and instead independently verifies only the cross-reference and the Legislature's supplement-not-supersede statement that appear in section 86 itself. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was located for the existence of this cross-reference. Whether a court applying section 6104 in a specific will or trust contest actually applies the section 15610.70 factors, as opposed to relying purely on common-law undue-influence doctrine, is a question of case law this clause does not resolve.

WHO MAY OBJECT, AND HOW A PRE-PROBATE CONTEST PROCEEDS
Standing to raise most of these grounds turns on being an "interested person" -- a term California law defines to include an heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, or anyone else with a property right in or claim against the estate that the proceeding may affect, as well as anyone with priority for appointment as personal representative, or a fiduciary representing an interested person; the statute adds that exactly who qualifies can vary with the specific proceeding and purpose involved. Where a will is contested before it is admitted to probate, the contestant files a written objection to probate with the court in Sacramento County County, a summons then issues and is served together with a copy of that objection, and the summons must direct the persons served to file a written response within 30 days of service.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), “interested person” includes any of the following: (1) An heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against a trust estate or the estate of a decedent which may be affected by the proceeding. (2) Any person having priority for appointment as personal representative. (3) A fiduciary representing an interested person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 48 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, definition of "interested person" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=48.)
  "(a) When a will is contested under Section 8004, the contestant shall file with the court an objection to probate of the will. Thereafter, a summons shall be issued and served, with a copy of the objection, on the persons required by Section 8110 to be served with notice of hearing of a petition for administration of the decedent’s estate. The summons shall be issued and served as provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 412.10) and Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 413.10) of Title 5 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The summons shall contain a direction that the persons summoned file with the court a written pleading in response to the contest within 30 days after service of the summons."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8250(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, pre-admission will contest procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8250.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standing concept and the pre-admission contest procedure -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim that every ground described in this document requires "interested person" status in every proceeding type. The "interested person" definition (Cal. Prob. Code section 48) and the pre-admission contest procedure (Cal. Prob. Code section 8250(a)) are two independently-numbered sections in different divisions of the Probate Code, not subsections of one; each was independently verified. This clause does not state the separate rule for contesting the appointment of a personal representative (section 8004(a)), and does not cover the rule that a person named as executor has no duty to defend a contest until appointed (section 8250(b)).

DEADLINE TO CONTEST AFTER A WILL HAS ALREADY BEEN ADMITTED
Once a will has already been admitted to probate, a separate deadline applies to raising these grounds: an interested person may petition to revoke that probate within 120 days after the will was admitted, unless that person was already a party to a will contest or had actual notice of one in time to have joined it. California law carves out one exception to that 120-day deadline: a person who was a minor, or who was incompetent and had no guardian or conservator, when the will was admitted to probate may petition to revoke the probate at any time before the court enters an order for final distribution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "(a) Within 120 days after a will is admitted to probate, any interested person, other than a party to a will contest and other than a person who had actual notice of a will contest in time to have joined in the contest, may petition the court to revoke the probate of the will. The petition shall include objections setting forth written grounds of opposition. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a person who was a minor or who was incompetent and had no guardian or conservator at the time a will was admitted to probate may petition the court to revoke the probate of the will at any time before entry of an order for final distribution."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8270 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, 120-day deadline to petition to revoke probate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8270.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 8270), used as real evidence of the actual post-admission deadline and its minor/incompetent exception -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim about when any particular estate's final distribution will occur. Both the 120-day deadline (section 8270(a)) and the minor/incompetent exception (section 8270(b)) are subsections of the same statutory section, disclosed here as the same source rather than as independent corroboration of each other. This clause's own citation is independent, however, of the pre-admission standing-and-procedure clause elsewhere in this document, which draws on separately-numbered sections 48 and 8250.

A TRUST CONTEST RUNS ON A DIFFERENT CLOCK
A trust contest does not automatically follow the same procedural timeline as a will contest. Where a revocable trust, or part of one, becomes irrevocable because a settlor died, California law requires the trustee to serve a formal notification on each beneficiary of the now-irrevocable trust and on each heir of the deceased settlor. Once that notification has been served, the recipient may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days after the notification was served, or, if a copy of the trust's terms is later delivered during that 120-day window, more than 60 days after that delivery -- whichever of the two deadlines is later.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 16061.7, whether the notice is served on the person within or after the time period set forth in subdivision (f) of Section 16061.7, shall not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification by the trustee is served upon the person, or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered pursuant to Section 1215 to the person during that 120-day period, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.8 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, 120/60-day trust contest deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.8.)
  "(a) A trustee shall serve a notification by the trustee as described in this section in the following events: (1) When a revocable trust or any portion thereof becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, trustee's duty to serve the triggering notification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a trust contest runs on its own notice-triggered deadline rather than automatically sharing the will-contest deadlines described elsewhere in this document -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim that every trust contest is subject to this deadline (a trust that never becomes irrevocable by a settlor's death, or for which no notification is ever served, is not addressed by this clause, nor is standing to bring a trust contest). The 120/60-day deadline itself comes from Cal. Prob. Code section 16061.8; the trustee's duty to serve the notification that starts that clock comes from a separate section, section 16061.7(a)(1) -- these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one, though they are substantively linked (one creates the triggering notice, the other states the deadline it triggers), which is disclosed here rather than presented as two unrelated confirmations of the identical fact. This clause does not assume that the "interested person" / procedural concepts used elsewhere in this document for will contests apply identically to a trust contest.

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I certify that I have read this information sheet on the substantive grounds recognized under California law for contesting a will or trust, and on the standing and time-limit rules described in it, and that this sheet states facts about the law generally rather than advising me on whether any ground applies to particular facts or on what to do about my own situation.

Signed: _______________________ Date: September 1, 2026
At: Oakland, California
